title: Pacific Christianity
hook: from Fiji to Samoa, village churches fill with harmony on Sunday

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dalit Christians, and a hand that reached out on the road, and your line was no one untouchable.

Sunday morning, a village on a Pacific island. The shops are shut. The road is quiet. Then, from a white church near the water, the singing starts. No organ, no screen with the words. Just voices, men low, women high, parts weaving over and under each other, so full the windows seem to hum. A visitor stands outside and doesn't want to go in, in case it stops. In Samoa, in Tonga, in Fiji, Sunday has a sound.

The gospel came to the Pacific by ship, with missionaries from Britain and elsewhere. That story has its hard chapters, as mission stories often do, tangled with trade and empire. But it didn't stay a foreign thing. Islanders themselves became the teachers and pastors, and some sailed on to other islands, carrying the faith in their own languages. Some island readers find their place already named in the Psalms. In the King James Bible: "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof." Isaiah says it too: "Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof." Hymns arrived with the missionaries, and island singers took them somewhere new, folding in their own ways of singing in many parts at once. A Tongan or Samoan choir doesn't just perform a hymn. It builds one, voice by voice. That's the quiet lesson inside harmony. In unison, everyone sings the same note. In harmony, everyone sings a different note, and the notes fit. No one voice carries the song alone; if the basses drop out, everyone hears the hole. The letter to the Colossians tells an early church to be "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." One another. Singing, in that letter, is something a church does together, not something it watches.
screen: `LET THE MULTITUDE OF ISLES BE GLAD.`
`A CHOIR BUILDS A HYMN, VOICE BY VOICE.`

segments.voice: Hum the first line of a hymn, or any song that has carried you somewhere, low in your chest. Hum it again and listen to the room around you, the fridge, traffic, a bird, and notice how your note sits among them, one part of a larger sound. If you pray, let the humming be your prayer, or say the psalm's line, let the multitude of isles be glad; if not, simply keep humming, and listen.
Pacific Christianity. The faith of Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and the islands around them, carried island to island by islanders, and sung in many parts at once.
Your line: the island choirs. Different notes, and every one of them fits. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: In Pacific island churches, Sunday worship is often marked by full congregational and choir singing in several parts, frequently without instruments, and in some island villages Sunday itself is kept as a day of rest.

chat.says: How did Christianity in the Pacific islands become the islanders' own?
options: Islanders became the pastors, carried it island to island, and sang it their own way.
Missionaries from Britain kept leading every church there, so it stayed theirs.
Islanders kept the hymns exactly as the missionaries sang them, note for note.
chat.meaning: It came by ship with missionaries, but islanders became teachers and pastors, sailed it on in their own languages, and sang the hymns in many parts.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'whole islands sing in harmony' was softened in the hook field and script ('village churches fill with harmony', 'Sunday has a sound'). No dates or numbers given.

'missionaries from Britain and elsewhere' (London Missionary Society, Wesleyan Methodists and others) and 'Islanders themselves became the teachers and pastors, and some sailed on to other islands' (Pacific Islander missionaries, e.g. from Samoa, Tonga, Cook Islands, Fiji): general; confirm. 'their own canoes' is a loose image; confirm or change to 'boats'.
'as mission stories often do, tangled with trade and empire': a brief honest note on colonial context; confirm tone.
Choir singing in many parts, often unaccompanied, in Tongan, Samoan and Fijian churches: general description; confirm.
howItsDone: 'Sunday ... kept as a day of rest in island villages' is a generalization; soften if needed.
